title: How to mirror dockerhub with artifactory
author: spuder

posts.author: spuder
posts.text:
Since dockerhub has started limiting downloads for non-paid accounts, I am frequently getting this error

ERROR: Preparation failed: Error response from daemon: toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit. You may increase the limit by authenticating and upgrading: https://www.docker.com/increase-rate-limit (executor_docker.go:188:15s)

https://docs.docker.com/docker-hub/download-rate-limit/

I have an artifactory server, how can I setup docker to cache/mirror from artifactory first?

posts.author: spuder
posts.text:
First setup an artifactory remote that points to docker hub at https://registry-1.docker.io

Then reconfigure all docker agents to use the registry_mirror. There are multiple ways to do this, but adding --registry-mirror to the docker start up options is most likely the easiest. See the docker documentation for more information

https://docs.docker.com/registry/recipes/mirror/

Method 1

Add --registry-mirror to the OPTIONS variable in /etc/default/docker

cat /etc/default/docker
OPTIONS=" -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock --ip-forward=true --iptables=true --ip-masq=true --registry-mirror=https://docker.artifactory.example.com -G docker"

Method 2

Edit /etc/docker/registry/config.yml

proxy:
  remoteurl: https://registry-1.docker.io
  username: [username]
  password: [password]

Method 3

If using puppet the config looks like this

  class { '::docker':
    use_upstream_package_source => false,
    manage_package              => false,
    registry_mirror             => 'https://docker.artifactory.example.com',
  }

posts.author: John Peterson
posts.text:
Steps to avoid running into Dockerhub rate limits:

-
Sign up for a Dockerhub free account if you do not already have one. Dockerhub enables credential pulls of up to 200 per 6 hours vs 100 per 6 hours for anonymous pulls.

-
Use Artifactory as a cache between Dockerhub by setting up a remote repo to Dockerhub and a local repo to push and pull images that are not on dockerhub.

-
Avoid using Dockerhub for personal images. Only pull official images as necessary.

-
Setup your docker clients to always pull through Artifactory by using the docker repo path of the virtual repo ex:

docker.artifactory.example.com/docker-virtual/myimage:1.0.0

-
Pull official images the same way by using the path w/ the virtual repo in it.

docker.artifactory.example.com/docker-virtual/ubuntu:latest

-
Monitor your Dockerhub rate limits through the use of analytics JFrog has provided integrations into Splunk, Elastic, and Prometheus to monitor your rolling 6 hour window of dockerhub pull requests and cache hit ratio.

posts.author: Eldad Assis
posts.text:
You can also get some information in an official blog JFrog released related to this.

See detailed instructions from @john-peterson in this page.

posts.author: Yves Martin

title: Docker login replacement when using buildctl
author: deez

posts.author: deez
posts.text: I'm running buildctl inside my k8s pod to build an image. Since docker socket doesn't exist anymore I can't use docker login with my credentials. Is there a way to login to docker hub so I won't hit any rate limits when pulling images without using docker login command ?

posts.author: BMitch
posts.text:
Buildkit doesn't depend on the docker engine. It is reading the credentials directly from the config file:

If credentials are required, buildctl will attempt to read Docker configuration file $DOCKER_CONFIG/config.json. $DOCKER_CONFIG defaults to ~/.docker.

Source: https://github.com/moby/buildkit

So if you mount a docker login secret into the container where you run the buildctl command, it should be used.

title: Gcloud Instances have no Docker Hub RateLimit
author: Kim

posts.author: Kim
posts.text:
Recently Docker introduced rate limit for the Docker Hub: https://docs.docker.com/docker-hub/download-rate-limit

On my local machine and DigitalOcean I can see these in action when running:

TOKEN=$(curl "https://auth.docker.io/token?service=registry.docker.io&scope=repository:ratelimitpreview/test:pull" | jq -r .token)

curl --head -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/ratelimitpreview/test/manifests/latest 2>&1 | grep RateLimit

I see for example:

RateLimit-Limit: 500;w=21600
RateLimit-Remaining: 491;w=21600

But this isn't the case when running this on a fresh GCP Gcloud instance. There the headers for RateLimit are not returned. Any idea why this could be?

posts.author: DazWilkin
posts.text:
At least 2 alternatives:

-
Google's infrastructure is (inadvertently) stripping the headers

-
Docker is not (applying the limits adding the headers) to requests from Google's blocks

I suspect the latter is more probable because Docker may be concerned at unintentionally rate limiting by (shared) IPs. However, I tried an authenticated (to Docker) test too and that could have utilized my identity but to rate limit me but that did not include the headers in the response either.

If you suspect the former, you should submit a support ticket to Google and have a support engineer trace the request for you.

NOTE I used a Cloud Shell VM

posts.author: Paolo Mainardi
posts.text:
I don't think that it was working because there were some internal caches instead, it was part of an internal agreement between Docker and GCP, as reported here

We are now having several issues with GKE clusters and the docker hub pull rate limit, when the token is not configured, even before 15 July everything works as expected.

title: How to cache docker images in gitlab with dind or dood
author: Janning Vygen

posts.author: Janning Vygen
posts.text:
On your own machine Docker downloads images once and uses them again and again. But on Gitlab CI, things look a little different. Usually you use a docker-in-docker Container called dind which downloads the images and runs them, but after the pipeline did run, the dind Container is removed and so are all images which have been downloaded.

This is a problem because of the speed of the pipeline, but also because of docker hub rate limit.

How to achive better performance and avoid hitting the rate limit

posts.author: Janning Vygen
posts.text:
Possible Solutions are:

-
Dependency Proxy

-
Docker Registry Mirror

-
Mounting /var/lib/docker

-
docker-out-of-docker

-
RECOMMENDED: docker save/load and gitlab Cache

Dependency Proxy

In Gitlab you can easily use a Dependency Proxy which is well documented.

imageproxy:
    stage: build
    image: ${CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_DIRECT_GROUP_IMAGE_PREFIX}/alpine:latest
    script: date

After running this pipeline you can see the image in your Dependency Proxy if you navigate in the Gitlab UI to your Group and then to "Operate/Dependency Proxy"

This is helpful if you only want to avoid the docker hub rate limit. But it does not help so much with performance. Check out these four jobs. We use a very heavy image (in terms of MByte) to have it more realistic:

proxy-off:
  stage: build
  # image is cached in the host docker as the image is defined as a job property,
  image: cypress/browsers:22.17.0
  script: date

proxy-on:
  stage: build
  # image is cached in the host docker, so using a proxy does only help for docker rate limit
  image: ${CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_DIRECT_GROUP_IMAGE_PREFIX}/cypress/browsers:22.17.0
  script: date

dind-proxy-off:
  stage: build
  image: docker:latest
  script:
    - docker run --rm cypress/browsers:22.16.0 date

dind-proxy-on:
  stage: build
  image: docker:latest
  script:
    - echo "$CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_PASSWORD" | docker login ${CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_SERVER} --username ${CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_USER} --password-stdin
    - docker run --rm ${CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_DIRECT_GROUP_IMAGE_PREFIX}/cypress/browsers:22.16.0

All these jobs take 45 Seconds in my machine the first time they ran.

The second time proxy-of and proxy-on took 8 seconds. But not because of the proxy, but because the docker image is cached on the host machine as the docker on the host machine is running that image if defined in the job specification. These jobs are not using docker-in-docker

the jobs with "dind" are just saving a few seconds at best, if the connection to docker hib is much much slower than to your own server. Be aware that even if downloading is faster, the image must be extracted which takes a lot of time too.

If you repeat these jobs without any cach, you have to delete the Dependency Proxy Cache (via Gitlab UI) and run docker image prune -fa (Be aware: this delete all images on your host machine)

Docker Registry Mirror

The docker Registry Mirror has the same problems as the proxy. It is not faster, but avoids Docker hub rate limit.

Mounting /var/lib/docker

Another Option is to configure your gitlab-runner/config.toml and mount the directory /var/lib/docker like this:

 volumes = ["/certs/client", "/cache", "/var/lib/docker"]

This way the dind Service is using the same Directory for saving images as the docker host

See here under "Inner docker image caching": https://blog.nestybox.com/2020/10/21/gitlab-dind.html

Don't do this because:

By making the containerized Docker’s image cache persistent, you are not just persisting images downloaded by the containerized Docker daemon; you are persisting the entire state of that Docker daemon (i.e., stopped containers, volumes, networks, etc.)

A given host volume bind-mounted into a system container’s /var/lib/docker must only be mounted on a single system container at any given time.

docker-out-of-docker

You can use docker-out-of-docker (dood) to let the host docker engine run all your docker jobs. You need to mount the socket in your gitlab-runner/config.toml, like this:

volumes = ["/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock", "/cache"]

Then

test:
  stage: build
  variables:
    DOCKER_HOST: unix:///var/run/docker.sock
  image: docker:latest
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache docker-cli
  script:
    - docker run --rm cypress/browsers:22.16.0 date

This works fine and uses the docker on your host machine and therefore the image cache. But as your job itself is running inside a container you can't mount any project files. So, if you want to build your app or want your docker container to do anything with your project files, you need to bind mount the files, like this:

test:
  stage: build
  variables:
    DOCKER_HOST: unix:///var/run/docker.sock
  image: docker:latest
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache docker-cli
  script:
    - docker run --rm -v "$(pwd):/app" cypress/browsers:22.16.0 la -alR /app

But the directory $(pwd) is now referring to the host machine, so nothing is mounted. You can't access your files.

Best Solution: docker load/save

This is the best solution I found so far:

services:
  - name: docker:28-rc-dind
    command: [ '--tls=false', '--host=tcp://0.0.0.0:2376' ]

dindImageCache:
  stage: build
  image: docker:latest
  cache:
    key: "dockerimages"
    paths:
      - dockerimages
  before_script:
    - |-
      for image in postgres:13.6 nginx:1.29.0 cypress/browsers:22.17.0 grafana/k6:0.54.0
      do
        FILE="dockerimages/$image"
        if [ -e $FILE ]
        then
          docker load -i $FILE
        else
          mkdir -p $(dirname $FILE)
          docker pull $image
          docker save -o $FILE $image
        fi
      done

dind-cache-on:
  stage: build
  image: docker:latest
  script:
    - docker run --rm cypress/browsers:22.17.0 date

The cache can be reused across all jobs and pipelines. If a tar file is found, it will get loaded into the dind docker engine. This is much faster than fetching it from a registry.

You can easily test it by changing the cache key to something else, so all images are downloaded and extracted again.

On my machine I save 50 seconds of execution time (for these four images above)
